### Energy efficiency

We perform the same heterogeneity analysis on EPC letter. We plot the coefficients on the interaction between EPC letter and adopting Cosy. As before, we hightlight that these coefficients do not include the direct impact of better EPC on energy consumption. We do not find strong differences in ability to switch energy consumption away from peak to Cosy periods by EPC (houses with a lower EPC rating seem to be able to shift less in the morning and peak, but the differences are not statistically significant). As a word of caution, EPC might not reflect well heatloss, most houses in our datasets have a EPC rating of D or above and people that have adopted Cosy might know their ability to shift prior to adoption. 


```{r epc-plot, eval=FALSE}
m2a <- feols(consumption_hh ~ i(cosy_contract_active, epc_letter, ref=0)  | 
               daily_avg_heating_degree + date + account_id,
             data = aggregated_data, 
             split = ~ rate_period,
             cluster = ~account_id)

# Define colors to match the Energy Efficiency Rating chart
rating_colors <- c(
  "A" = "#00CC00",  # Green
  "B" = "#66FF33",  # Light Green
  "C" = "#FFFF00",  # Yellow
  "D" = "#FF9900",  # Orange
  "E" = "#FF6600",  # Dark Orange
  "F" = "#FF0000",  # Red
  "G" = "#990000"   # Dark Red
)

for (i in 1:5) {
  # Find model
  val <- m2a[[i]]$model_info$sample$value
  j <- which(sapply(1:5, function(j) m1[[j]]$model_info$sample$value) == val)
  
  # Extract coefficients and standard errors
  coefs <- coeftable(m2a[[i]]) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    separate(term, into = c("cosy_contract_active", "remove1", "EPC letter", "remove2"), sep = "::") %>%
    mutate(lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`
    )
  # Assuming coefs is your data frame and rating_colors is your color vector
  coefs <- coefs %>%
    mutate(EPC_label_position = max(Estimate) * 0.1)  # Position for EPC labels on the right
  
  # Create the ggplot
  ggplot(coefs, aes(y = rev(factor(`EPC letter`)), x = Estimate, fill = factor(`EPC letter`))) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci), width = 0.2, color = "grey") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +  # Add vertical line at x = 0
    geom_vline(xintercept = m1[[j]]$coefficients, linetype = "dashed", color = cosy_color, alpha=0.6) +  # Add vertical line at ATE
    geom_text(aes(x = EPC_label_position, label = `EPC letter`), hjust = 0, color = "white") +  # Add EPC letters on the right
    scale_fill_manual(values = rating_colors, name = "EPC Letter") +  # Use the defined colors+
    labs(
      x = "Average Half Hourly Consumption",
      y = "EPC Letter"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_blank(),  # Hide original y-axis text
      axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),  # Hide original y-axis ticks
      axis.text.y.right = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  # Center the text on the right-hand side
      axis.title.y.right = element_text(margin = margin(l = 10)),  # Add margin to right y-axis title
      legend.position = "none"  # Remove legendx
    )
  
  
  # Print the plot
  ggsave(paste0("../graphs/epc_", val %>% tolower() %>% str_replace(" ", "_"), ".png"),
         width = 16, height = 8, units = "cm")
}

# Assuming m2a is your model list, m1 contains the ATE values, and rating_colors is your color vector
all_coefs <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:5) {
  # Find model
  val <- m2a[[i]]$model_info$sample$value
  j <- which(sapply(1:5, function(j) m1[[j]]$model_info$sample$value) == val)
  
  # Extract coefficients and standard errors
  coefs <- coeftable(m2a[[i]]) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    separate(term, into = c("cosy_contract_active", "remove1", "EPC_letter", "remove2"), sep = "::") %>%
    mutate(
      average = m1[[j]]$coefficients,
      lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * Std..Error,
      upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * Std..Error,
      `%_ATE` = Estimate / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      lower_ci_ATE = lower_ci / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      upper_ci_ATE = upper_ci / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      period = val
    )
  
  # Combine all coefficients
  all_coefs <- bind_rows(all_coefs, coefs)
}

# Assuming coefs is your data frame and rating_colors is your color vector
all_coefs <- all_coefs %>%

    axis.text.y.right = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  # Center the text on the right-hand side
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(margin = margin(l = 10)),  # Add margin to right y-axis title
    legend.position = "none"  # Remove legend
```

### Heatloss

In order to look more closely whether or not houses with poorer insulation can provide flexibility, we use a subset of customers for which Octopus Energy has calculated their heatloss rate.

As before, we plot the interaction between heatloss rate decile and adopting Cosy. We find that houses with greater heatloss rate have more heating to shift around, meaning that they are able to shift more energy consumption away from peak rate to cosy periods. On ther hand, houses with low rate of heatloss are barely able to shift any heating around. The only impact of adopting Cosy is through the decrease in peak consumption observed at any temperature. 


```{r heatloss}

# Create unique breaks for predicted_heatloss_watts
breaks <- unique(quantile(aggregated_data[!is.na(aggregated_data$predicted_heatloss_watts),]$predicted_heatloss_watts/1000, probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)))

# Create pretty labels for the categories
labels <- sapply(1:(length(breaks)-1), function(i) paste0(round(breaks[i], 1), " kW to ", round(breaks[i+1], 1), " kW"))

# Create the categories for predicted_heatloss_watts
aggregated_data <- aggregated_data %>%
  mutate(predicted_heatloss_watts_category = cut(predicted_heatloss_watts/1000, 
                                                 breaks = breaks, 
                                                 include.lowest = TRUE,
                                                 labels = labels))


m_heatloss <- feols(consumption_hh ~ i(cosy_contract_active, predicted_heatloss_watts_category, ref =0) 
                    | date +  account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree,
                    data = aggregated_data %>% filter(!is.na(predicted_heatloss_watts_category)),
                    split = ~ rate_period,
                    cluster = ~account_id)

for (i in 1:5) {
  
  # Find model
  val <- m_heatloss[[i]]$model_info$sample$value
  j <- which(sapply(1:5, function(j) m1[[j]]$model_info$sample$value) == val)
  
  # Extract coefficients and standard errors for total_consumption
  coefs_total <- coeftable(m_heatloss[i]) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    separate(coefficient, into = c("cosy_contract_active", "remove1", "Heatloss MW Category", "remove2"), sep = "::") %>%
    mutate(lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           outcome = "Total Consumption") %>%
    mutate(`Heatloss MW Category` = factor(`Heatloss MW Category`, levels = labels))
  
  # Define the shades of reds
  red_palette <- c("#FF9999", "#FF8080", "#FF6666", "#FF4D4D", "#FF3333", "#FF1A1A", "#FF0000", "#E60000", "#CC0000", "#B20000")
  
  # Create the ggplot
  ggplot(coefs_total, aes(x = `Heatloss MW Category`, y = Estimate, fill = `Heatloss MW Category`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), width = 0.2, color = "grey") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +  # Add horizontal line at y = 0
    geom_hline(yintercept = m1[[j]]$coefficients, linetype = "dashed", color = cosy_color, alpha = 0.6) +  # Add horizontal line at ATE
    scale_fill_manual(values = red_palette) +
    labs(
      x = "Heatloss MW Decile",
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Estimate (kWh)", 
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ./m1[[j]]$coefficients, name = "% of ATE", labels = scales::percent_format())
      
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),  # Tilt x-axis labels for better readability
      legend.position = "none"  # Remove legend
    )
  
  # Print the plot
  ggsave(paste0("../graphs/heatloss_", val %>% tolower() %>% str_replace(" ", "_"), ".png"),
         width = 16, height = 8, units = "cm")
  
}


m_heatloss2 <- feols(share_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active, predicted_heatloss_watts_category, ref =0)
                     | date +  account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree,

                       group_by(account_id, date) %>%

                     split = ~ rate_period,

           upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           outcome = "Total Consumption") %>%
```
```{r floor-area}
    mutate(`Floor Area` = factor(`Floor Area`, levels = labels))
  
  # Define the shades of reds
  red_palette <- c("#FF9999", "#FF8080", "#FF6666", "#FF4D4D", "#FF3333", "#FF1A1A", "#FF0000", "#E60000", "#CC0000", "#B20000")

    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), width = 0.2, color = "grey") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +  # Add horizontal line at y = 0
    geom_hline(yintercept = m1_share[[j]]$coefficients, linetype = "dashed", color = cosy_color, alpha = 0.6) +  # Add horizontal line at ATE
    scale_fill_manual(values = red_palette) +
    labs(
      x = "Floor Area Decile",
      y = "Half Hourly Consumption in kWh"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "% of Daily Consumption",
      labels = scales::percent_format(),
      sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ./m1_share[[j]]$coefficients, name = "% of ATE", labels = scales::percent_format())
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),  # Tilt x-axis labels for better readability
      legend.position = "none"  # Remove legend
    )
  
  # Print the plot
  ggsave(paste0("../graphs/share_floor_area_", val %>% tolower() %>% str_replace(" ", "_"), ".png"),
         width = 16, height = 8, units = "cm")
  
}
```

```{r property-value}

# Create unique breaks for property_value
breaks <- unique(quantile(aggregated_data[!is.na(aggregated_data$property_value),]$property_value, 
                          probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)))

# Create pretty labels for the categories
labels <- sapply(1:(length(breaks)-1), function(i) paste0("£", round(breaks[i]/1000, 0), "k to £", 
                                                          round(breaks[i+1]/1000, 0), "k"))
labels[length(labels)] <- paste0("£", round(breaks[length(breaks)-1]/1000), "+")

# Create the categories for property_value
aggregated_data <- aggregated_data %>%
  mutate(property_value_category = cut(property_value, 
                                       breaks = breaks, 
                                       include.lowest = TRUE,
                                       labels = labels))


m_property_value <- feols(consumption_hh ~ i(cosy_contract_active, property_value_category, ref =0) 
                          | date +  account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree,
                          data = aggregated_data %>% filter(!is.na(property_value_category)),
                          split = ~ rate_period,
                          cluster = ~account_id)

m_property_value_share <- feols(share_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active, property_value_category, ref =0)
                                | date +  account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree,
                                data = aggregated_data %>% 
                                  filter(!is.na(property_value_category), !rate_period=="Overall") %>%
                                  group_by(account_id, date) %>%
                                  mutate(share_consumption = total_consumption/sum(total_consumption)),
                                split = ~ rate_period,
                                cluster = ~account_id)

# Initialize an empty data frame to store all coefficients

  # Find model

    data.frame() %>%

    mutate(lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           outcome = "Total Consumption",

                                              "Peak Rate",
                                              "Other", 
                                              "Overall")),

           average = m1[[j]]$coefficients)

  # Define the shades of reds

  ggplot(coefs_total, aes(x = `Property Value`, y = Estimate, fill = `Property Value`)) +

    ) +

    )
  
  # Print the plot
  ggsave(paste0("../graphs/property_value_", val %>% tolower() %>% str_replace(" ", "_"), ".png"),
         width = 16, height = 8, units = "cm")
  
}
```

### Regions

Finally, we plot the interaction between customers' regions and adopting Cosy. In this regressions, we control for days and customers fixed effects, and isolate the impact of adopting Cosy. We compare all regional differences to our omitted base region, East Midlands. 
We do not find any regional difference as shown in Table \@ref(tab:regionaldid).

```{r regions, eval=FALSE}

m_region <- feols(consumption_hh ~ i(cosy_contract_active, region, ref =0) 
                  | date +  account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree,
                  data = aggregated_data %>% filter(!is.na(region), !region==""),
                  split = ~ rate_period,
                  cluster = ~account_id)
etable(m_region, tex = TRUE, title = "Cosy Adoption by Region",
       label = "tab:regionaldid",
       fitstat = ~ N + g + pre_avg +t_obs + r2, 
       file = "../tables/did_region.tex", replace = TRUE)


# Extract coefficients for total consumption
all_coefs <- data.frame()
for (i in 1:5) {
  val <- m_region[[i]]$model_info$sample$value
  j <- which(sapply(1:5, function(j) m1[[j]]$model_info$sample$value) == val)
  
  coefs_total <- coeftable(m_region[[i]]) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    separate(term, into = c("cosy_contract_active", "remove1", "Region", "remove2"), sep = "::") %>%
    mutate(
      average = m1[[j]]$coefficients,
      lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
      upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
      `%_ATE` = Estimate / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      lower_ci_ATE = lower_ci / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      upper_ci_ATE = upper_ci / abs(m1[[j]]$coefficients) * 100,
      period = factor(val, levels = c("Morning Cosy",
                                      "Afternoon Cosy",
                                      "Peak Rate",
                                      "Other", 
                                      "Overall")))
  
  
  all_coefs <- bind_rows(all_coefs, coefs_total)
}

# Select a color palette from RColorBrewer
region_colors <- brewer.pal(n = length(unique(all_coefs$Region)), name = "Set3")

# Order regions by their estimate size for period == "Morning Cosy"
morning_cosy_order <- all_coefs %>%
  filter(period == "Morning Cosy") %>%
  arrange(desc(Estimate)) %>%
  pull(Region)

# Reorder the Region factor based on the estimate size in "Morning Cosy"
all_coefs <- all_coefs %>%
  mutate(Region = factor(Region, levels = morning_cosy_order))

# Create the ggplot
ggplot(all_coefs %>% filter(period != "Overall"), aes(x = Region, y = Estimate, fill = Region)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), width = 0.2, color = "grey") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +  # Add horizontal line at y = 0
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = average), linetype = "dashed", color = cosy_color, alpha = 0.6) +  # Add vertical line at average ATE
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors) +  # Apply random colors to regions
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),  # Tilt x-axis labels for better readability
    legend.position = "none"  # Remove legend
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ period)

# Save the plot
ggsave("../graphs/region_combined.png", device = "png", width = 16, height = 12, units = "cm")
```

```{r hpinstallation}
# Register the pre-treatment average fit statistic
fitstat_register("pre_avg3", function(x) {
  
  # Extract the formula
  formula <- x$fml_all$linear
  
  # Extract the outcome variable from the formula
  outcome_variable <- all.vars(formula)[1]
  
  # Extract the call object and evaluate the data argument
  call_object <- x$call
  data_expr <- call_object$data
  data <- eval(data_expr)
  
  # Get the logical vector of observations used in the model
  obs_used <- obs(x)
  
  # Subset the original dataset using this logical vector
  data_used <- data[obs_used, ]
  
  # Ensure the outcome variable is treated as a column name
  outcome_values <- data_used[[outcome_variable]]
  
  # Create pre-avg for non-HP installed group
  pre_avg <- mean(outcome_values[data_used$is_hp_installed == 1 & data_used$cosy_contract_active == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Format the pre-avg
  formatted_pre_avg <- format_decimal(pre_avg)
  
  return(formatted_pre_avg)
}, "Half Hourly Consumption Pre-Cosy")
```

# Conclusion {#sec:conclusion}

This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of the Cosy rate on electricity consumption patterns, utilizing the latest methods in staggered adoption analysis to ensure robust results. Our findings highlight several key points:

1. **Strong Effect on Shifting Consumption Away from Peak Periods:**
- The adoption of Cosy significantly shifts electricity consumption away from peak periods. This effect is evident throughout the year, indicating that Cosy effectively encourages users to avoid high-cost periods.

2. **Persistence Over Time:**
- The impact of Cosy adoption is persistent, demonstrating lasting changes in consumption behavior well beyond the initial adoption phase. This persistence underscores the potential for sustained demand-side management through time-of-use tariffs.

3. **Seasonal Variations:**
- The effects of Cosy are particularly pronounced during the winter months, where the shift in consumption is more substantial. However, there is also evidence of peak avoidance during other months, highlighting the versatility and effectiveness of the tariff across different seasons.

4. **Mor Flexibility for Houses with Higher Heatloss**
- Our analysis reveals that consumers with higher heatloss tend to shift their consumption more significantly than customers with better insulated houses. 

5. **Enhanced Shifting by Time-of-Use Tariff Users:**
- Customers who previously used time-of-use tariffs exhibit even greater shifts in their consumption patterns upon adopting Cosy. This finding suggests that these users are already accustomed to adjusting their usage in response to price signals, making them more adept at optimizing their consumption under the new tariff.

6. **Rigorous Analytical Methods:**
- Our study employs the most rigorous methods available for analyzing staggered treatment adoption, including the Callaway and Sant’Anna estimator and the Goodman-Bacon decomposition. These methods ensure that our results are robust and account for variations in treatment timing and heterogeneity in treatment effects.

In summary, the Cosy rate has a substantial and lasting impact on shifting electricity consumption away from peak periods, with particularly strong effects during the winter months. Larger consumers and those previously on time-of-use tariffs show the most significant shifts, indicating the potential for targeted demand-side management strategies.

## Goodman Bacon Decomposition {#sec:baconexplanation} {-}

In this section, we use the Goodman-Bacon Decomposition to understand the contributions of different sources of variation in a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) analysis. It decomposes the overall treatment effect estimated by DiD into its constituent parts, allowing researchers to identify which comparisons (such as those between treated and untreated groups at different times) drive the overall estimate.

To construct the Goodman-Bacon Decomposition, we need to restrict our dataset to customers for whom the treatment is increasing monotonically (people that switched to Cosy and stayed) and for whom we observe all treatment periods. Therefore, we limit our data to after October 2023. This gives us a dataset of 2814 customers. We aggregate the observations at the weekly level for ease of computing (there too many comparisons if we use daily adoption data). We show here the results for Peak Rate period analysis. 
Even with the restriction we had to impose, the two way fixed effect difference-in-differences estimates recreated from the Bacon decomposition (-8.97 kWh per week) is very close to the ones from our main analysis  (-1.244 kWh per day times 7 ~ -8.708 kWh per week). 

The Bacon decomposition summary is as follows:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Type & Weight & Avg\_ES \\
\midrule
\rowcolor{gray!10} Earlier vs Later Treated & 0.1411035 & -12.031270 \\
Later vs Always Treated & 0.6338757 & -7.531177 \\
\rowcolor{gray!10} Later vs Earlier Treated & 0.2204715 & -8.606004 \\
Treated vs Untreated & 0.0045493 & -6.535066 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


**Earlier vs Later Treated:** comparison shows a significant negative effect size, indicating that those treated earlier had a greater reduction in electricity consumption compared to those treated later. The weight suggests this comparison contributes 14.1% to the overall treatment effect.

**Later vs Always Treated:** is the most heavily weighted comparison, contributing 63.4% to the overall effect. It indicates that those treated later saw a reduction in consumption compared to those who were always treated, but the reduction is smaller than in the earlier vs later comparison.^[We have always treated customers in this sample as we add to reduce the window of analysis to construct a balance panel] 

**Later vs Earlier Treated:** comparison, contributing 22.0% to the overall effect, shows that later treated individuals had a significant reduction compared to earlier treated ones, though not as large as the earliest comparison. It is the closest to our two-way fixed effect  estimates (-1.244 kWh times 7 ~ -8.708 kWh per week). 

**Treated vs Untreated:** comparison, while only contributing 0.45% to the overall effect, shows the difference between treated and untreated customers, indicating a moderate reduction in consumption for treated customers.

The Goodman-Bacon Decomposition allows us to see how different comparisons contribute to the overall DiD estimate. A plot of all comparisons is also shown in Figures \@ref(fig:bacon1) and \@ref(fig:bacon2). In our case, the most substantial contributions come from comparisons involving **later treated versus always treated customers**, and **earlier versus later treated customers**. These results indicate that the timing of adopting Cosy plays a crucial role in the observed reduction in electricity consumption, with earlier adopters showing more significant reductions. Earlier adoptors would have also used Cosy during the 2022-2023 Winter enerhy crisis, potentially leading to larger shift in consumption. 

The next biggest contributors is the **Later vs Earlier Treated** with smaller coefficients. This comparison is incorrect:  The DiD approach relies on the assumption that the control group provides a valid counterfactual for the treated group. "Later vs Earlier Treated" directly compares units that receive the treatment at different times without considering the pre-treatment period for both groups. This comparison mixes the treatment effects from different time periods, violating the parallel trends assumption.

Motivated by the insights from the Goodman-Bacon decomposition and the need to properly account for staggered adoption, we apply the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) approach in Section \@ref(sec:santanna). This method accommodates treatment effect heterogeneity and corrects for timing differences, providing a more robust analysis of the treatment effects over different periods.

By using the Callaway and Sant'Anna approach, we can more accurately estimate the causal impact of Cosy adoption, ensuring that our results are not confounded by inappropriate comparisons and properly reflect the treatment effects across different groups and times.


```{r bacon-decomp}

if(!file.exists("../graphs/bacon_decompostion_subgroup.png")) {
  
  
  # Adjust your existing code to calculate 'week' and 'firstweek' as the number of weeks from the start_date
  did_data <- aggregated_data %>%
    inner_join(contract_analysis %>% select(account_id, category)) %>%
    filter(category == "Stayed on Cosy (ongoing)") %>%
    mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) %>%
    group_by(account_id, week, tariff_gsp_group_id, rate_period) %>%
    summarise(total_consumption = sum(total_consumption),
              cosy_contract_active = max(cosy_contract_active))
  
  rm(aggregated_data, weather)
  gc()
  
  # Get complete cases
  complete_case <- did_data %>% 
    filter(rate_period=="Peak Rate") %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(account_id, week, total_consumption, cosy_contract_active) %>%
    complete(account_id, week, fill=list(total_consumption=NA, cosy_contract_active=NA))
  
  # Identify account_ids with complete data for every date
  balanced_account_id <- complete_case %>% 
    filter(week > "2023-09-30") %>%
    group_by(account_id) %>%
    filter(all(!is.na(total_consumption))) %>%
    pull(account_id) %>%
    unique() 
  
  # Filter for balanced obs
  balanced_data <- did_data %>% 
    filter(week >= "2023-09-30") %>%
    filter(rate_period=="Peak Rate") %>%
    filter(account_id %in% (balanced_account_id))
  
  rm(adoption, complete_case, did_data)
  gc()
  
  # Bacon decomposition
  bacondecomp <- bacon(total_consumption ~ cosy_contract_active, 
                       data=balanced_data, 
                       id_var="account_id", 
                       time_var="week", 
                       quietly = F)
  
  
  ggplot(bacondecomp) +
    aes(x = weight,
        y = estimate,
        shape = factor(type),
        colour = factor(type)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, 
               linetype = "longdash") +
    labs(x = "Weight",
         y = "Estimate",
         shape = "Type",
         colour = "Type",
         theme_minimal() +
           theme(legend.position = "bottom")
         
         ggsave("../graphs/bacon_decomposition.png")
         
         
         
         # Export the table to LaTeX using kable and kableExtra
         bacondecomp %>%
           group_by(type) %>%
           summarise(weight = sum(weight),
                     avg_es = mean(estimate)) %>%
           kable("latex", booktabs = TRUE) %>%
           kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down")) %>%
           save_kable(file = "../tables/bacon.tex")
         
         # install.packages("forcats")
         
         # Adjust your dataset and graph
         bacondecomp %>%
           mutate(subgroup = paste0(treated, "_", untreated),
                  subgroup = factor(subgroup),
                  subgroup = fct_reorder(subgroup, estimate)) %>%
           group_by(type) %>%
           ggplot(aes(x = estimate, 
                      y = subgroup,
                      colour = type,
                      size = weight)) +
           geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +  # Add transparency
           geom_vline(xintercept = weighted.mean(bacondecomp$estimate, bacondecomp$weight),
                      linetype = "longdash") +
           theme_minimal() +
           theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +  # Remove y-axis labels
           labs(colour = "Type",
                size = "Weight",
                y = "",
                x = "Estimate")
         
         ggsave("../graphs/bacon_decompostion_subgroup.png")
}
```

## Share electricity consumption {-}

The table's analysis shows how adopting the Cosy rate plan impacts customers' electricity usage patterns across different times of the day, focusing on the change in the share of daily electricity consumption per period. 

- **Afternoon Cosy Period:** After switching to the Cosy rate, the proportion of electricity used during the afternoon cosy period increased by 6.62 percentage points. This indicates customers are more inclined to consume electricity during these hours under the Cosy rate.
- **Morning Cosy Period:** The adoption of the Cosy rate led to an even more pronounced increase in electricity use during the morning cosy period, with a 12.56 percentage point rise in its share of daily consumption. This suggests a significant behavioral shift towards consuming more electricity in the morning hours.
- **Other Times:** Contrarily, there's a decrease in the share of electricity consumption during times not designated as cosy by 14.71 percentage points, reflecting a shift away from electricity usage during these periods.
- **Peak Rate Times:** The share of daily electricity usage during peak rate times also saw a decrease, falling by 4.75 percentage points. This reduction implies that consumers are adjusting their usage to avoid higher-cost periods.

```{r gas, include=FALSE}
# Function to update HP detection status per hashed_mpan
update_hp_status <- function(data) {
  hp_status <- ifelse(is.na(data$HP), 0, data$HP)
  
  # Identify the first pair of consecutive detections (1,1)
  first_pair <- which(diff(hp_status) == 0 & hp_status[-1] == 1 & hp_status[-length(hp_status)] == 1)[1]
  
  if (!is.na(first_pair)) {
    # Go backwards to find the start of the sequence of consecutive 1s
    start_index <- first_pair
    
    while (start_index > 1 && hp_status[start_index] == 1) {
      start_index <- start_index - 1
    }
    
    # If the backward loop stops at a `0`, increment to the first `1`
    if (hp_status[start_index] == 0) {
      start_index <- start_index + 1
    }
    
    # Set all previous values up to start_index - 1 as 0
    hp_status[1:(start_index - 1)] <- 0
    
    # Set all subsequent values from start_index onwards to 1
    hp_status[start_index:length(hp_status)] <- 1
  }
  
  # Check for isolated detections and set them to 0 if not the most recent value
  detection_indices <- which(hp_status == 1)
  
  if (length(detection_indices) == 1 && detection_indices != length(hp_status)) {
    hp_status[detection_indices] = 0
  }
  
  return(hp_status)
}

# Apply the function to each hashed_mpan group
gas_readings <- gas_readings %>%
  group_by(hashed_mpan) %>%
  mutate(hp_detected = update_hp_status(cur_data())) %>%
  ungroup()

# Aggregate the number of HP for each date

  summarise(total_HP = sum(hp_detected, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
```

```{r monthlyelectrcity, eval=FALSE}
# Step 1: Extract the month number and determine the winter year
elec_readings <- elec_readings %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract the year from the date
    year = year(month_date),
    # Extract the month as a numerical value
    month_num = month(month_date),
    # Mark as winter if the month is within November to April
    is_winter = (month_num >= 11 | month_num <= 3),
    # Adjust the year for months from January to April to count them as previous year's winter season
    winter_year = ifelse(month_num <= 34, year - 1, year),
  ) %>%
  # Step 2: Filter for the winter months (Nov to Apr)
  filter(month_num >= 11 | month_num <= 3) %>%
  # Step 3: Calculate the average consumption per winter season for each hashed_mpan
  group_by(hashed_mpan, winter_year) %>%
  mutate(winter_avg = mean(monthly_consumption, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  # Step 4: Lag the winter averages
  group_by(hashed_mpan)%>%
  mutate(
    # Retrieve the previous winter's average
    prev_winter_avg = lag(winter_avg),
    # If previous winter avg is NA, set above_prev_winter to 0
    above_prev_winter = ifelse(is.na(prev_winter_avg) | (monthly_consumption <= prev_winter_avg + 150), 0, 1)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Function to update the detection indicator based on consecutive detections
update_hp_detection <- function(data) {
  hp_status <- data$above_prev_winter
  
  # Identify the first pair of consecutive detections (1,1)
  first_pair <- which(diff(hp_status) == 0 & hp_status[-1] == 1 & hp_status[-length(hp_status)] == 1)[1]
  
  if (!is.na(first_pair)) {
    # Set all values before the first pair to 0
    hp_status[1:first_pair] = 0
    
    # Set all values from the first pair onwards to 1
    hp_status[(first_pair + 1):length(hp_status)] = 1
  }
  
  # Handle isolated detections that are not at the end
  detection_indices <- which(hp_status == 1)
  if (length(detection_indices) == 1 && detection_indices != length(hp_status)) {
    hp_status[detection_indices] = 0
  }
  
  return(hp_status)
}

# Function to adjust the date to the next November 1st or current year if already past November
adjust_to_next_winter <- function(date) {
  year_value <- year(date)
  month_value <- month(date)
  
  if (month_value > 4 & month_value < 11) {
    return(as.Date(paste0(year_value, "-11-01")))
  } else {
    return(as.Date(date))
  }
}
```

In this section, I use a sample of Cosy customers that had their heat pump installed by Octopus Energy Service to create an algorythm that detects heat pump installation and apply it to the larger sample. 

The data consists of electricity and gas consumption for 69 customers, tracked from 2018 to 2024. The data is available only for those periods when the customers had active accounts with Octopus Energy. Alongside the consumption data, we also have the exact date pf the installation of heat pumps for these customers. Utilizing this data, we employed a machine learning algorithm to identify the timing of heat pump installations and apply it to the larger sample of Cosy customers. 

### Data Preparation and Feature Engineering

The data used includes monthly electricity and gas readings, weather conditions, and installation records. The target is whether or not an Heat Pump is installed for a particular month. At this point, the script is not recursive - meaning that I did not apply it recursively - a customer can have an heat pump detected in January but not April. In spite of this simplication, the algorythm is still quite successful at accuretely detecting heatpumps. 

For the heat pump detection algorithm, significant preprocessing steps were taken to enrich the data and make it suitable for machine learning analysis. This included creating rolling averages of gas and electricity consumption to smooth out short-term fluctuations and highlight longer-term trends, which are more indicative of a heat pump’s operation. I also calculated differences between consecutive months' readings to capture sudden changes in consumption patterns potentially indicating the installation of a heat pump.

```{r importanceplot, include=TRUE, fig.cap= "Importance plot from the random forest model", out.width = '60%', fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("../graphs/importance.png")
```

### Algorithm Implementation
The core of the approach was a Random Forest Classifier, a robust machine learning model suitable for classification tasks. The classifier was trained on features such as rolling averages of consumption, consumption, monthly differences in consumption, weather-related variables, and installation data. These features were chosen to effectively distinguish between periods before and after a heat pump installation based on changes in energy usage patterns influenced by the efficiency and operational characteristics of heat pumps.

### Model Training and Evaluation
After splitting the data into training and test sets (70% versus 30% given our small sample size), we trained the Random Forest model on the training data, tuning it to identify the presence of a heat pump installation. The model's performance was evaluated on the test dataset using a confusion matrix, which provided a clear picture of its accuracy in correctly identifying actual installations versus non-installations.


### Confusion Matrix
The performance of our heat pump detection algorithm, evaluated through the confusion matrix and associated statistics, provides a comprehensive view of its effectiveness. Here’s a detailed breakdown of the results from the model evaluation:

- **True Negatives (TN):** 387 cases where the model correctly predicted the absence of a heat pump installation.
- **False Positives (FP):** 15 cases where the model incorrectly predicted a heat pump installation.
- **False Negatives (FN):** 16 cases where the model failed to detect an existing heat pump installation (these are concentrated druing summer months as shown in Figure \@ref(fig:predovertime)).
- **True Positives (TP):** 174 cases where the model correctly identified the presence of a heat pump installation.


```{r predovertime, include=TRUE, fig.cap= "Prediction Types over Time", out.width = '60%', fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("../graphs/predictions_over_time.png")
```




### Model Accuracy and Statistics
The overall accuracy of the model was 94.76%, which indicates that the classifier was able to correctly identify the presence or absence of heat pump installations in a high percentage of cases. The 95% confidence interval for the accuracy is between 92.65% and 96.41%, suggesting a high level of precision in the model’s predictions.

### Additional Statistical Measures

- **No Information Rate (NIR):** This is the accuracy that could be achieved by always predicting the most frequent class. Here, it is 68.07%, significantly lower than the model's accuracy, indicating that the model's predictions are not merely by chance (P-Value < 2e-16).
- **Kappa Statistic:** The Kappa value of 0.8797 suggests a very good agreement between the predictions and the actual installations, correcting for the accuracy of random chance.
- **Mcnemar's Test:** The P-value of 1 for Mcnemar's test indicates that the model's performance is stable across different subsets of the dataset, with no significant bias between the type I and type II errors.

### Sensitivity and Specificity
- **Sensitivity (Recall):** The model has a sensitivity of 96.03%, meaning it correctly identifies 96.03% of the actual installations. This high sensitivity is crucial for ensuring that most heat pump installations are detected.
- **Specificity:** With a specificity of 92.06%, the model effectively identifies 92.06% of cases where no heat pump has been installed, minimizing the instances where installations are falsely detected.

### Predictive Values
- **Positive Predictive Value (Precision):** The precision of 96.27% indicates that when the model predicts a heat pump installation, it is correct 96.27% of the time.
- **Negative Predictive Value:** The negative predictive value of 91.58% shows the probability that the absence of a detected installation truly means no installation.

### Balanced Accuracy
- **Balanced Accuracy:** At 94.05%, the balanced accuracy, which is the average of sensitivity and specificity, indicates excellent model performance in both detecting installations and confirming non-installations.

These metrics collectively demonstrate that the model is highly effective at distinguishing between the presence and absence of heat pump installations in the dataset.

### Limtations of the Current Model

While the results from the model are highly encouraging, there are some limitations in the current approach that are important to consider for future research and operational improvements:

1. **Skewed Distribution of Installations:**
A significant limitation in the current dataset is that most heat pump installations occurred after 2022. This skewness can introduce bias into the model, as it might overfit to the characteristics of more recent data. It could affect the model's ability to generalize effectively across other time periods or predict future trends accurately, especially if the market conditions or regulatory frameworks around energy use and equipment installation change.

2. **Small Sample Size:**
The dataset consists of only 69 customers, which limits the statistical power of the analysis and increases the likelihood of overfitting. With such a small sample, the model's ability to capture the full variability in consumer behavior and installation effects across different demographics and geographic locations is constrained. This can impact the robustness and scalability of the model when applied to a broader population.

### Future Plans to Enhance the Model

Recognizing these limitations, there are plans to expand the dataset and refine the modeling approach:

1. **Increasing the Dataset Size:**
To address the issue of a small sample size and improve the model’s generalizability, the dataset will be expanded beyond just 'Cosy' rate adopters. This expansion will include a wider range of customers who have installed heat pumps, regardless of their rate plan. By broadening the scope of the data, the model will benefit from a more diverse set of consumption patterns and installation timelines, enhancing its accuracy and reliability.

2. **Incorporating a More Diverse Set of Data:**
Using smart tariff survey will allow us to also use the data from customers that have their heat pump installed further in the past and with different providers. This will not only reduce the potential bias from the current dataset’s concentration of recent installations but also enable the model to adapt to a more diverse heat pump users population.

```{r detact-hp-install, eval=FALSE}
# load weather data [needs to be expanded]

  mutate(month_date = floor_date(delivery_from, "month")) %>%
  rename(tariff_gsp_group_id = gsp_group_id) %>%
  group_by(month_date) %>%
  summarise(avg_heating_degree = mean(avg_heating_degree),
            temperature = mean(avg_air_temperature_celsius),
            wind = mean(avg_wind_speed),
            cloud = mean(avg_cloud_cover_total)) 

# merge back with electricity readings
elec_readings <- elec_readings  %>%
  inner_join(weather) 

# Read data and ensure date is handled correctly
gas_readings <- fread("../data/input/cosy_-_gas_readings_2024_05_07.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert the latest_reading_read_at column to a Date type
    date = as.Date(latest_reading_read_at),
    # Extract the year from the date
    year = year(date),
    # Extract the month as a numerical value
    month_num = month(date),
    # Mark as winter if the month is within November to April
    is_winter = (month_num >= 11 | month_num <= 3),
    # Adjust the year for months from January to April to count them as previous year's winter season
    winter_year = ifelse(month_num <= 3, year - 1, year),
    # Create a new column representing the start of the month
    month_date = floor_date(date, "month")
  )  %>%
  # Rename and select only relevant columns
  rename(gas_consumption = corrected_consumption) %>%
  select(hashed_mpan, month_date, gas_consumption, winter_year, is_winter) 

consumption_data <- gas_readings %>%
  # Join with other data if needed
  right_join(elec_readings, by=c("hashed_mpan", "month_date")) %>%
  mutate(gas_consumption = ifelse(gas_consumption == 99999 | is.na(gas_consumption), 0, gas_consumption),
         gas_consumption = round(gas_consumption)) %>%
  left_join(fread("../data/input/COSY HP Install 2024 May 08.csv")) %>%
  mutate(is_installed = as.integer(heat_pump_installed_at <= month_date))


# Step 2: Preprocessing and feature engineering
merged_data <- consumption_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(heat_pump_installed_at)) %>%
  mutate(
    gas_rolling_avg = zoo::rollapply(gas_consumption, width = 3, FUN = mean, align = "right", fill = NA),
    elec_rolling_avg = zoo::rollapply(elec_consumption, width = 3, FUN = mean, align = "right", fill = NA),
    gas_diff = c(NA, diff(gas_consumption)),
    elec_diff = c(NA, diff(elec_consumption))
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))) %>%
  ungroup()

# Select the relevant features for model input
features <- merged_data %>%
  select(gas_rolling_avg, elec_rolling_avg, elec_consumption, gas_consumption, avg_heating_degree, gas_diff, elec_diff, is_installed, month_date, tariff_gsp_group_id, is_winter)

# Step 3: Train-Test Split
set.seed(123)
split_indices <- sample(seq_len(nrow(features)), size = 0.7 * nrow(features))

train_data <- features[split_indices, ]
test_data <- features[-split_indices, ]

train_features <- train_data %>%
  select(-is_installed)
train_target <- train_data$is_installed

test_features <- test_data %>%
  select(-is_installed)
test_target <- test_data$is_installed

# Step 4: Model Training (Random Forest Classifier)
model <- train(
  train_features, as.factor(train_target),
  method = "rf",
  ntree = 100
)

# Step 5: Model Evaluation
predictions <- predict(model, test_features)
confusion_matrix <- confusionMatrix(predictions, as.factor(test_target))

# Feature importance plot (from the random forest model)
importance <- varImp(model, scale = FALSE)


# Create the plot
importance_plot <- ggplot(importance, aes(x = reorder(Variables, Overall), y = Overall)) +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Features", y = "Importance")

# Save the plot
ggsave("../graphs/importance.png", plot = importance_plot)

# Prepare a data frame with the original test data and predictions
results <- data.frame(
  month_date = test_data$month_date,
  Actual = test_target,
  Predicted = predictions
)

# Function to classify predictions into true positive, false positive, etc.
get_prediction_type <- function(actual, predicted) {
  if (actual == 1 && predicted == 1) {
    return("True Positive")
  } else if (actual == 0 && predicted == 1) {
    return("False Positive")
  } else if (actual == 1 && predicted == 0) {
    return("False Negative")
  } else {
    return("True Negative")
  }
}

# Apply the function to classify each row
results$PredictionType <- mapply(get_prediction_type, results$Actual, results$Predicted)

# Summarize by month
monthly_summary <- results %>%
  group_by(month_date, PredictionType) %>%
  summarize(Count = n(), .groups = 'drop')

# Plot using ggplot2
ggplot(monthly_summary %>% filter(month_date >= "2023-05-01"), aes(x = month_date, y = Count, color = PredictionType, shape = PredictionType, group = PredictionType)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "True Positive" = 16,  # Filled circle
      "True Negative" = 17,  # Filled triangle
      "False Positive" = 1,  # Empty circle
      "False Negative" = 2   # Empty triangle
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Count",
    color = "Prediction Type",
    shape = "Prediction Type"
  )

# Save the plot
ggsave("../graphs/predictions_over_time.png")


```

```{r attachedpredictions, eval=FALSE}
# Prepare the features from the original merged dataset (ensure the same feature engineering is applied)
merged_data <- consumption_data %>%
  group_by(hashed_mpan) %>%
  # Mark as installed if heat pump was installed before or on this monthly period
  mutate(
    is_installed = ifelse(!is.na(heat_pump_installed_at) & heat_pump_installed_at <= month_date, 1, 0),
    gas_rolling_avg = zoo::rollapply(gas_consumption, width = 3, FUN = mean, align = "right", fill = NA),
    elec_rolling_avg = zoo::rollapply(elec_consumption, width = 3, FUN = mean, align = "right", fill = NA),
    gas_diff = c(0, diff(gas_consumption)),
    elec_diff = c(0, diff(elec_consumption))
  ) %>%
  # Replace any remaining missing numeric values with 0 or another appropriate imputation method
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))) %>%
  mutate(tariff_gsp_group_id = ifelse(is.na(tariff_gsp_group_id), "_A", tariff_gsp_group_id),
         # Extract the month as a numerical value
         month_num = month(month_date),
         # Mark as winter if the month is within November to April
         is_winter = (month_num >= 11 | month_num <= 3)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Extract the features for prediction
predict_features <- merged_data %>%
  select(gas_rolling_avg, elec_rolling_avg, elec_consumption, gas_consumption, avg_heating_degree, gas_diff, elec_diff, month_date, tariff_gsp_group_id, hashed_mpan, is_winter)

# Make predictions using the trained model
predictions <- predict(model, predict_features)

# Add predictions back to the dataset
predict_features$predicted_is_installed <- (predictions)

# Check the first few rows to confirm predictions are attached
predict_features <- predict_features %>%
  inner_join(consumption_data %>% select(hashed_mpan, month_date, is_installed)) %>%
  group_by(hashed_mpan) %>%
  mutate(
    # Step 1: Prioritize `is_installed` if not missing
    predicted_is_installed = ifelse(!is.na(is_installed), is_installed, predicted_is_installed),
    # # Step 2: Propagate `1` if it was present in a previous month for this `hashed_mpan`
    # predicted_is_installed = cummax(predicted_is_installed)
  ) %>%
  group_by(hashed_mpan) %>%
  filter(predicted_is_installed==1) %>%
  summarise(pred_installed_at = min(month_date))


# Aggregate the number of HP for each date
predict_features %>%
  group_by(pred_installed_at) %>%
  tally() %>%
  # Plot the aggregated data using a bar chart
  ggplot(aes(x = as.Date(pred_installed_at), y = n)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "blue") +
  scale_x_date(
    labels = scales::date_format("%b %y"),  # Formatting months and years
    date_breaks = "3 month"  # Adjust this based on your data density
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "Total HP"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)  # Improve readability by rotating labels
  )

ggsave("../graphs/predicted_HP_installations.png")

# join the predicted install back to the original daily data
aggregated_data <- aggregated_data %>%
  left_join(predict_features %>%
              select(hashed_mpan, pred_installed_at)) %>%
  mutate(month_date = floor_date(date, "month"),
         predicted_is_installed = date >= pred_installed_at) 


# Check the impact of HP installation
m1 <- feols(elec_consumption ~ i(predicted_is_installed, ref=0) | account_id + month_date + avg_heating_degree, 
            data = consumption_data %>%
              inner_join(predict_features)%>%
              mutate(predicted_is_installed = as.numeric(month_date >= pred_installed_at)) %>%
              filter(is_winter),
            cluster = ~ account_id)


etable(m1, tex=TRUE, title = "Impact of Predicted Heat Pump Installations (restricted to winter months)",
       label="tab:hp-impact",
       fitstat = ~ N + g + pre_avg +t_obs + r2, file = "../tables/hp_impact.tex", replace = TRUE)
```

### Predicting the Impact of Heat Pump Installations

To assess the impact of predicted heat pump installations on energy consumption, we extended our analysis to the larger sample of Cosy customers, incorporating the predictions from our machine learning algorithm. We plot the predicted monthly installations in Figure \@ref(fig:timeplothpinstall). We then constructed a regression model to estimate the effects of predicted heat pump installations on monthly electricity consumption. The results are summarized in Table \ref{tab:hp-impact}. We focused on the winter months, as this period is most likely to exhibit significant changes in energy usage patterns due to heating demands.

The regression analysis shows that the installation of a heat pump is associated with a significant increase in monthly electricity consumption by 236.2 kWh, as indicated by the coefficient with a significance level of 0.01 (***). The fixed-effects model accounts for variations across individual customers (account_id), months, and average heating degree days, ensuring that the observed effects are robust and not driven by unobserved heterogeneity.

\input{"../tables/hp_impact.tex"}

## Event study {-}

We run the following model by period for all customers that have adopted Cosy in the past year: 

$$Consumption_{it} = \sum^W _{w={-52, -9, ..., 1, ..,52}} \alpha_w WeeksSinceCosy^w_{it} + X\beta + \delta_t +  \gamma_i +  \epsilon_{it} $$
where:
- $WeeksSinceCosy^w_{it}$  is a categorical variable equals to the number of weeks before and after the adoption of Cosy. We use the week prior adoption as omitted category. 

The charts show the event study coefficients for each specified period. We find that coefficients are consistent with those from the difference-in-differences analysis for the Morning and Afternoon Cosy periods.

Interestingly, the pre and opost trends don't appear to be as stable, almost indicating an overall decrease/increase in consumption overtime per period. 


```{r event-study-period,  include=TRUE,  fig.cap= "Event Study Analsyis", out.width = '60%', fig.align="center"}

library(dplyr)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)


# Define the rate periods you want to analyze
rate_periods <- unique(aggregated_data$rate_period)

# Function to process and plot for a single rate period
process_and_plot <- function(period) {
  event_study_df <- aggregated_data %>%
    mutate(weeks_since_cosy = case_when(
      weeks_since_cosy < -52 ~ -52,
      weeks_since_cosy > 52 ~ 52,
      TRUE ~ weeks_since_cosy
    )) %>%
    filter(rate_period == period) %>%
    select(c(account_id, weeks_since_cosy, consumption_hh, daily_avg_heating_degree, daily_avg_air_temperature_celsius, date))
  
  # Fixed-effects regression
  est_did <- feols(consumption_hh ~ i(weeks_since_cosy, -1)  | 
                     date + account_id + daily_avg_heating_degree, 
                   data = event_study_df,
                   cluster = ~account_id)
  
  # Extract coefficients and standard errors
  coefs <- coeftable(est_did) %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    separate(term, into = c("var", "weeks_since_cosy"), sep = "::") %>%
    mutate(lower_ci = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           upper_ci = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
           outcome = "Half Hourly Consumption") %>%
    mutate(weeks_since_cosy = as.numeric(weeks_since_cosy),
           post = (weeks_since_cosy > -1))
  
  # Create the plot
  plot <- ggplot(coefs, aes(x = weeks_since_cosy, y = Estimate, color = post)) +
    geom_point(stat = "identity", show.legend = TRUE) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), width = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
    labs(
      x = "Weeks Since Cosy Adoption",
      y = "Half Hourly Consumption in kWh",
      color = "Cosy"  # Update legend title
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c("TRUE" = cosy_color, "FALSE" = flexible_color),  # Set custom colors
      labels = c("No", "Yes")  # Update legend labels
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),  # Tilt x-axis labels for better readability
      legend.position = "bottom"  # Show legend
    )
  
  # Save the plot
  ggsave(paste0("../graphs/event_study_", gsub(" ", "_", tolower(period)), ".png"),
         plot = plot, width = 16, height = 8, units = "cm")
}


# Apply the function to each rate period
purrr::walk(rate_periods, process_and_plot)
```

```{r}
  mutate(settlement_period = ifelse(settlement_period >48,

sample_hashed_mpans <- sample(unique_hashed_mpans, 1000)


hourly_df <- hourly_df %>%
  filter(hashed_mpan %in% sample_hashed_mpans,
         !is.na(settlement_period)) %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(interval_start),
    time = format(interval_start, format = "%H:%M:%S")
  )

checks <- hourly_df %>%
  group_by(settlement_period, time) %>%
  tally()

gc()

m_hourly <- feols(consumption ~ i(settlement_period, ref=1) +
                    i(settlement_period, pre_post_cosy, ref2="pre") 
                  | hashed_mpan + settlement_date,
                  cluster = ~ hashed_mpan,
                  data = hourly_df)

# midnight consumption
midnight <- hourly_df %>% 
  filter(settlement_period==1, pre_post_cosy=="pre") %>% 
  summarise(mean_consumption = mean(consumption, na.rm = TRUE))

# Extract coefficients and standard errors
coefs <- coeftable(m_hourly) %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  separate(term, into = c("remove", "ubeube", "settlement_period", "is_cosy"), sep = ":") %>%
  mutate(settlement_period = as.numeric(settlement_period),
         adjusted_estimate = Estimate + midnight$mean_consumption,
         lower_ci = adjusted_estimate - 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
         upper_ci = adjusted_estimate + 1.96 * `Std..Error`,
         cosy = ifelse(!is.na(is_cosy), "Yes", "No")
  ) %>%
  filter(settlement_period <= 48)

# Add the row for settlement_period == 1, is_cosy == NA, and Estimate == midnight$mean_consumption
midnight_row <- tibble(
  settlement_period = 1,
  is_cosy = NA,
  Estimate = midnight$mean_consumption,
  Std..Error = 0,
  lower_ci = midnight$mean_consumption,
  upper_ci = midnight$mean_consumption,
  cosy = "No",
  adjusted_estimate = midnight$mean_consumption,
  remove = NA
)

# Calculate adjusted estimates and confidence intervals
coefs <- coefs %>%
  group_by(settlement_period) %>%
  arrange(cosy) %>%
  mutate(
    adjusted_estimate = ifelse(cosy == "Yes" & settlement_period>1, Estimate + first(Estimate) + midnight$mean_consumption, 
                               Estimate + midnight$mean_consumption),
    lower_ci = adjusted_estimate - 1.96 * Std..Error,
    upper_ci = adjusted_estimate + 1.96 * Std..Error
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Bind the midnight_row to the coefs dataframe
coefs <- bind_rows(midnight_row, coefs)


# Function to convert settlement period to time
settlement_period_to_time <- function(period) {
  hours <- (period - 1) %/% 2
  minutes <- ifelse((period %% 2) == 1, "00", "30")
  sprintf("%02d:%s", hours, minutes)
}

# Apply the function to create time labels
coefs <- coefs %>%
  mutate(time_label = settlement_period_to_time(settlement_period))

# Apply the function to create time labels
coefs <- coefs %>%
  mutate(time_label = settlement_period_to_time(settlement_period))

# Select a few representative time labels to display for clarity
selected_periods <- seq(min(coefs$settlement_period), max(coefs$settlement_period), by = 2)
display_labels <- coefs %>%
  filter(settlement_period %in% selected_periods) %>%
  distinct(settlement_period, time_label) %>%
  pull(time_label)

# Ensure breaks and labels have the same length
selected_periods <- coefs %>%
  filter(settlement_period %in% selected_periods) %>%
  distinct(settlement_period) %>%
  pull(settlement_period)

# Custom colors from the provided image

cosy_color <- "#fe49da"      # Replace with the exact hex code for Cosy

# Create the ggplot

  annotate("rect", xmin = 9, xmax = 14, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.2, fill = cosy_color) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 27, xmax = 32, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.2, fill = cosy_color) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 33, xmax = 38, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.2, fill = "red") +

    values = c("No" = flexible_color, "Yes" = cosy_color)  # Custom colors
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Time",
    y = "Half Hourly Consumption in kWh"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),  # Rotate x-axis labels for better readability
    legend.position = "bottom"  # Place legend on the right
```

```{r non-smart-tariff}
m1 <- feols(total_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active) | daily_avg_heating_degree + account_id + date, 
            data = aggregated_data, 
            cluster = ~account_id, 
            split = ~ rate_period)


m1_control <- feols(total_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active) | daily_avg_heating_degree + hashed_mpan + date, 
                    data = hp_installed, 
                    cluster = ~hashed_mpan, 
                    split = ~ rate_period)

etable(m1, m1_control)

etable(c(m1[1], m1_control[1],
         m1[2], m1_control[2],
         m1[3], m1_control[3],
         m1[4], m1_control[4]), tex=TRUE, title = "Cosy Adoption in kWh per day",
       headers = list(list("Afternoon Cosy"=2,
                           "Morning Cosy"=2,
                           "Other"=2,
                           "Peak Rate"=2),
                      list(rep(c("Cosy", "All HP users"), times=4))),
       fitstat = ~ N + g + pre_avg +t_obs + r2, file = "../tables/non-smart-tariff.tex", replace = TRUE, label="tab:non-smart-tariff")


# same coefficient but then control is pretty small/ variations come from the adopters
```



```{r non-smart-tariff2}

hp_installed <- fread("../data/input/cosy_-_hp_aggregated_up_2024_06_03.csv") %>%
  filter(hashed_mpan %in% unique(aggregated_data$hashed_mpan)) %>%
  rename(total_consumption=total_read_value,
         date = settlement_date) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date),
         is_hp_installed = heat_pump_installed_at <= date) 

weather <- fread("../data/input/Cosy Analysis Weather Mar 26 daily.csv") %>% 
  rename_with(.cols = starts_with("weekly"), 
              .fn = ~ sub("^weekly", "daily", .)) %>%
  rename(tariff_gsp_group_id=gsp_group_id) %>%
  mutate(date_day=as.Date(date_day, format = "%Y-%m-%d")) %>%
  rename(date = date_day)

hp_installed <- hp_installed %>%
  left_join(weather) %>%
  inner_join(aggregated_data %>% select(hashed_mpan, date, cosy_contract_active) %>% distinct()) %>%
  mutate(cosy_contract_active = ifelse(is.na(cosy_contract_active), 0, cosy_contract_active))


m1_hp <- feols(total_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active) + is_hp_installed | daily_avg_heating_degree + hashed_mpan + date, 
               data = hp_installed, 
               cluster = ~hashed_mpan, 
               split = ~ rate_period)

m1_hp2 <- feols(total_consumption ~ i(cosy_contract_active) | daily_avg_heating_degree + hashed_mpan + date, 
                data = hp_installed, 
                cluster = ~hashed_mpan, 
                split = ~ rate_period)

etable(m1, m1_hp, m1_hp2)

# same coefficient but then control is pretty small/ variations come from the adopters
```

In February 2018, Octopus Energy launched the first smart time of use tariff, Agile Octopus. Unlike other suppliers, Octopus Energy's systems have been designed for smart time of use tariffs, unlocked by smart meters and half hourly settlement.

Launched in early 2022, Intelligent Octopus Go takes smart charging to the next level, and is the UK's first 100% flexible charging tariff - providing drivers with six hours of low cost charging each night.
